cards.text: Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly when some edges have negative weights.
cards.explanation: A negative edge can make a distance that was already settled wrong. Use Bellman-Ford when weights can be negative.

cards.text: Breadth-first search finds the fewest edges from the start to every reachable node.
cards.explanation: It visits nodes level by level, so the first time it reaches a node is by the fewest edges.

cards.text: Breadth-first search keeps its waiting nodes in a stack.
cards.explanation: It uses a queue: first in, first out. A stack belongs to depth-first search.

cards.text: Depth-first search can be written with recursion or with an explicit stack.
cards.explanation: The recursion uses the call stack in the same way as an explicit stack.

cards.text: Kruskal's algorithm starts by sorting the edges by weight.
cards.explanation: It then tries the lightest edge first.

cards.text: Prim's algorithm grows one tree from a start node.
cards.explanation: At each step it adds the cheapest edge that joins the tree to a new node.

cards.text: A spanning tree of a connected graph with n nodes has n - 1 edges.
cards.explanation: Fewer edges leave a node out; more edges make a cycle.

cards.text: Bellman-Ford can detect a negative cycle.
cards.explanation: If an edge can still be relaxed after n - 1 rounds, a negative cycle exists.

cards.text: Floyd-Warshall finds the shortest distance between every pair of nodes.
cards.explanation: It fills a table of all pairs, one middle node at a time.

cards.text: Floyd-Warshall takes time proportional to the cube of the number of nodes.
cards.explanation: It has three nested loops over the nodes, so it runs in O(V^3).

cards.text: Merge sort takes O(n log n) time even in its worst case.
cards.explanation: It always halves the list and merges, whatever the order of the input.

cards.text: Quick sort takes O(n log n) time in every case.
cards.explanation: Its worst case is O(n^2), for example with a bad pivot on sorted input. Its average case is O(n log n).

cards.text: The usual merge sort sorts a list without any extra memory.
cards.explanation: Merging needs a second array of about the same size.

cards.text: Randomized quick sort picks its pivot at random so no input is always bad for it.
cards.explanation: A random pivot makes the bad case unlikely for every input.

cards.text: One run of Karger's algorithm always finds a minimum cut.
cards.explanation: One run finds a minimum cut only with some probability. The runs are repeated and the best cut is kept.

cards.text: In Karger's algorithm, contracting an edge merges its two end nodes.
cards.explanation: The merged node keeps the other edges; edges between the two ends disappear.

cards.text: Edmonds-Karp looks for augmenting paths with breadth-first search.
cards.explanation: Choosing the path with the fewest edges bounds the number of rounds.

cards.text: In a flow network, the value of the maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut.
cards.explanation: This is the max-flow min-cut theorem.

cards.text: In the 0/1 knapsack problem you may take part of an item.
cards.explanation: Each item is taken whole or left out. Taking parts is the fractional knapsack.

cards.text: Taking items by the best value per weight is optimal for the fractional knapsack.
cards.explanation: The greedy choice works because an item can be cut to fill the bag exactly.

cards.text: Taking items by the best value per weight is always optimal for the 0/1 knapsack.
cards.explanation: Whole items can leave unused room, so greedy can lose. Dynamic programming gives the best answer.

cards.text: The dynamic programming table for 0/1 knapsack has about items times capacity cells.
cards.explanation: There is one cell for each item count and each capacity.

cards.text: In a proper colouring, two neighbouring nodes may have the same colour.
cards.explanation: Neighbouring nodes must have different colours.

cards.text: A graph with no edges can be coloured with one colour.
cards.explanation: No two nodes are neighbours, so one colour is enough.

cards.text: Dijkstra's algorithm with a binary heap runs in O((V + E) log V) time.
cards.explanation: Each edge may push one entry on the heap, and each push or pop costs O(log V).

cards.text: Breadth-first search visits all neighbours of the start before the neighbours of those neighbours.
cards.explanation: That is the level-by-level order.

cards.text: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles.
cards.explanation: Remove any edge of a tree and it falls into two parts.

cards.text: When some edge weights tie, Prim and Kruskal can give different trees with the same total weight.
cards.explanation: The minimum spanning tree may not be unique, but its total weight is.

cards.text: Kruskal's algorithm skips an edge whose ends are already connected.
cards.explanation: Adding it would make a cycle.

cards.text: Kruskal's algorithm uses union-find to check whether two nodes are already connected.
cards.explanation: Union-find answers that question in almost constant time.

cards.text: Dijkstra's algorithm settles a node as soon as it is first put in the queue.
cards.explanation: A node is settled when it is taken out with the smallest distance, not when it is first queued.

cards.text: The basic Bellman-Ford algorithm relaxes every edge up to n - 1 times.
cards.explanation: A shortest path has at most n - 1 edges, so n - 1 rounds are enough.

cards.text: Quick sort that always takes the first element as pivot is slow on a list that is already sorted.
cards.explanation: Every split leaves one side empty, so the time grows to O(n^2).

cards.text: Merge sort is a divide and conquer algorithm.
cards.explanation: It splits the list, sorts the halves and merges them.

cards.text: Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm is defined for directed graphs in the same way as for undirected graphs.
cards.explanation: A minimum spanning tree is defined for undirected graphs. GraphLab asks for an undirected graph.

cards.text: An augmenting path is a path from the source to the sink that still has spare capacity.
cards.explanation: Pushing flow along it increases the total flow.

cards.text: Floyd-Warshall can handle negative edge weights if there is no negative cycle.
cards.explanation: It only needs the path lengths to be well defined.

cards.text: Depth-first search always finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
cards.explanation: It may find a long path first. Breadth-first search finds the shortest one.

cards.text: On a graph where every edge weighs 1, Dijkstra and breadth-first search give the same distances.
cards.explanation: Both settle the nodes in order of their distance.

cards.text: Find the shortest road route from one city to another. All distances are positive.
cards.explanation: Dijkstra finds the shortest weighted route when no weight is negative. Kruskal builds a tree, and breadth-first search counts edges, not distance.

cards.text: Join every village with the least total length of cable.
cards.explanation: Joining all nodes with the least total weight is a minimum spanning tree, which Kruskal builds.

cards.text: Find the fewest links between two people in a friendship network. Every link counts as 1.
cards.explanation: With equal links, the fewest links is found by breadth-first search.

cards.text: Some edges are negative, for example refunds. You need the shortest paths from one source.
cards.explanation: Bellman-Ford allows negative edges. Dijkstra can give wrong answers with them.

cards.text: You need the shortest distance between every pair of 40 stations.
cards.explanation: Floyd-Warshall fills the distances of all pairs in one run.

cards.text: Find how much water a pipe network can carry from the source to the city.
cards.explanation: Pipes have capacities, so this is a maximum flow problem. Edmonds-Karp solves it.

cards.text: Pack a bag with the most value. Each item must be taken whole or left out.
cards.explanation: Whole items mean the 0/1 knapsack, solved by dynamic programming.

cards.text: Fill a truck with grain and sugar that can be poured in any amount, for the most value.
cards.explanation: Goods that can be split suit the fractional knapsack: take the best value per weight first.

cards.text: Give exam slots to subjects so that two subjects with a shared student never share a slot, using few slots.
cards.explanation: Subjects are nodes, shared students are edges, and slots are colours: graph colouring.

cards.text: Sort a very large list and you need a time of O(n log n) that is guaranteed.
cards.explanation: Merge sort keeps O(n log n) in the worst case. Quick sort can fall to O(n^2).

cards.text: Sort a list in memory. You want a fast average time and very little extra memory.
cards.explanation: Quick sort sorts in place with a fast average time. Merge sort needs a second array.

cards.text: Estimate the minimum cut of a network quickly by choosing edges at random.
cards.explanation: Karger's algorithm contracts random edges, and repeated runs find the minimum cut with high probability.

cards.text: Check whether a maze has any route from the entrance to the exit by going as deep as possible before backing up.
cards.explanation: Going deep and backing up is depth-first search.

cards.text: Visit every room level by level, nearest first, starting at the entrance.
cards.explanation: Level by level, nearest first, is breadth-first search.

cards.text: Quick sort is slow on your sorted data. Which change makes the bad case unlikely for every input?
cards.explanation: Choosing the pivot at random gives randomized quick sort.

cards.text: Start in one house and always add the cheapest cable to a house that is not connected yet.
cards.explanation: Growing one tree by the cheapest edge to a new node is Prim's algorithm.

cards.text: Take the cheapest road from a sorted list, but skip any road that closes a loop.
cards.explanation: Sorting the edges and skipping cycles is Kruskal's algorithm.

cards.text: Check whether a chain of currency exchanges can earn money in a loop (a negative cycle).
cards.explanation: Bellman-Ford can report a negative cycle. Dijkstra cannot.

cards.text: How many cars per hour can go from the stadium to the highway through roads that each have a limit?
cards.explanation: Limits on roads make a flow network. The answer is its maximum flow.

cards.text: Find the fewest moves a robot needs on a grid, where each step costs the same.
cards.explanation: Equal steps mean the fewest moves are found by breadth-first search.

cards.text: Choose study topics. Each has a time cost and gives marks, and half a topic is not allowed. You want the most marks.
cards.explanation: Whole topics with a limit on time form a 0/1 knapsack.

cards.text: You need the fastest route from the capital to all other cities. Travel times are positive.
cards.explanation: One source and positive weights: Dijkstra.

cards.text: Combine two already sorted lists of results into one sorted list efficiently.
cards.explanation: The merge step of merge sort does exactly this in linear time.

cards.text: Colour a map so that countries that touch have different colours.
cards.explanation: Countries are nodes and borders are edges: graph colouring.

cards.text: Connect islands with bridges of different costs so that every island is reachable at the least cost.
cards.explanation: Connecting all nodes at the least cost is a minimum spanning tree. Prim builds one.

cards.text: Find the smallest set of links whose removal cuts the source from the sink, using a flow.
cards.explanation: By the max-flow min-cut theorem, a maximum flow also gives the minimum cut.

cards.text: Find all the nodes in the same connected piece as a start node, following each branch as far as it goes.
cards.explanation: Following each branch to its end is depth-first search.

cards.text: Find the distance, in edges, from one node to all others in O(V + E) time.
cards.explanation: Breadth-first search gives the edge distance to every node in linear time.

cards.text: Sort records and keep records with equal keys in their original order (a stable sort).
cards.explanation: Merge sort is stable. The usual quick sort is not.

cards.text: Find the shortest paths from one node when edge weights are zero or positive.
cards.explanation: Non-negative weights and one source: Dijkstra.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: BFS, DFS and Dijkstra all walk through a graph. Merge sort sorts a list of numbers.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Three of them sort a list. Dijkstra finds shortest paths in a graph.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall find shortest distances. Kruskal builds a spanning tree.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Three of them sort a list. The 0/1 knapsack chooses items for a bag.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Dijkstra, Kruskal and Prim use the weights on the edges. BFS only counts the number of edges (hops).

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Kruskal, Prim and the fractional knapsack are greedy: they take the best choice now. Merge sort divides and conquers.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Three of them split a list and sort the parts (divide and conquer). Kruskal is greedy.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: BFS, Prim and Dijkstra keep a queue of waiting nodes or edges. DFS goes deep first and uses a stack (recursion).

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: The first three build the answer from answers to smaller problems. The fractional knapsack is greedy: it sorts by value per weight.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Dijkstra, BFS and Bellman-Ford start from a chosen node. Kruskal needs no start node, because it looks at all edges.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Kruskal, Prim and BFS each end with a tree. Floyd-Warshall ends with a table of distances.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: BFS, Dijkstra and Kruskal always give the same answer on the same graph. Karger picks edges at random, so runs can differ.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: Merge sort, quick sort and DFS call themselves (recursion). Kruskal is a plain loop over the sorted edges.

cards.text: Which one does not belong with the other three?
cards.explanation: The first three find shortest distances. Edmonds-Karp finds a maximum flow.

cards.text: Match each algorithm with what it does.
pairs: Finds shortest paths when no edge is negative
Builds a cheapest spanning tree by sorting the edges
Visits the nodes in order of their hops from the start
Splits a list in halves and merges them back sorted
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Dijkstra is finds shortest paths when no edge is negative; Kruskal is builds a cheapest spanning tree by sorting the edges; BFS is visits the nodes in order of their hops from the start; Merge sort is splits a list in halves and merges them back sorted.

cards.text: Match each data structure with how it works.
pairs: Tells whether two nodes are in the same set
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Queue is first in, first out; Stack is last in, first out; Priority queue is the smallest key leaves first; Union-find is tells whether two nodes are in the same set.

cards.text: Match each algorithm with its family.
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Kruskal is greedy; Merge sort is divide and conquer; 0/1 knapsack is dynamic programming; Graph colouring is backtracking.

cards.text: Match each algorithm with its job.
pairs: Random contractions find a small cut
Maximum flow by shortest routes with spare room
Shortest paths even with negative edges
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Karger is random contractions find a small cut; Edmonds-Karp is maximum flow by shortest routes with spare room; Floyd-Warshall is shortest distances between all pairs; Bellman-Ford is shortest paths even with negative edges.

cards.text: Match each algorithm with its cost.
pairs: About n log n steps in every case
About n squared steps in its worst case
Looks at each node and each edge once
Three nested loops over the nodes
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Merge sort is about n log n steps in every case; Quick sort is about n squared steps in its worst case; BFS is looks at each node and each edge once; Floyd-Warshall is three nested loops over the nodes.

cards.text: Match each algorithm with how it works.
pairs: Grows one tree from a start node
Joins many small sets into one
Settles the closest node that is not settled yet
Relaxes every edge in repeated passes
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Prim is grows one tree from a start node; Kruskal is joins many small sets into one; Dijkstra is settles the closest node that is not settled yet; Bellman-Ford is relaxes every edge in repeated passes.

cards.text: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: Improving a distance by using one more edge
A route that comes back to its start
Joins all nodes with no cycle
Spare room left on an edge of a flow
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Relaxation is improving a distance by using one more edge; Cycle is a route that comes back to its start; Spanning tree is joins all nodes with no cycle; Residual capacity is spare room left on an edge of a flow.

cards.text: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: The element a quick sort part is split around
One round over all edges in Bellman-Ford
A route from source to sink with spare capacity
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Pivot is the element a quick sort part is split around; Pass is one round over all edges in Bellman-Ford; Augmenting path is a route from source to sink with spare capacity; DP table is stores answers to smaller problems.

cards.text: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: The best step now, never reconsidered
The best answer is built from best smaller answers
The least capacity that separates source from sink
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Negative cycle is makes shortest distances undefined; Greedy choice is the best step now, never reconsidered; Optimal substructure is the best answer is built from best smaller answers; Minimum cut is the least capacity that separates source from sink.

cards.text: Match each algorithm with its key idea.
pairs: Needs a table over items and room
Goes back when no colour fits
A random pivot avoids the sorted-input worst case
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Fractional knapsack is greedy by value per weight; 0/1 knapsack is needs a table over items and room; Graph colouring is goes back when no colour fits; Randomized quick sort is a random pivot avoids the sorted-input worst case.

cards.text: Match each algorithm with its key fact.
pairs: May need many runs to find the true minimum cut
Keeps a priority queue of edges
Fails when an edge is negative
cards.explanation: Each term goes with the meaning next to it in this list: Karger is may need many runs to find the true minimum cut; Prim is keeps a priority queue of edges; Kruskal is needs sorted edges and union-find; Dijkstra is fails when an edge is negative.

cards.text: Match each algorithm with the kind of answer it gives.
pairs: A spanning tree of least weight
cards.explanation: BFS gives the fewest edges from the start; Kruskal gives a spanning tree of least weight; quick sort gives a sorted list; Edmonds-Karp gives a maximum flow.
